issues.quote: He does it every year. He tells each person what is wrong with theirs.
issues.fact: The fact sheet says only that the master made everyone show their watches at nine. It gives no habit, no annual ritual, and no remarks about faults.
issues.misreading: A solver could read this as a regular routine that shows the master checks and corrects watches. That suggests the watches were already known to be off, which the sheet does not say.

issues.quote: Mine was exact. I regulated it myself.
issues.fact: The sheet says only that her watch was exact at nine.
issues.misreading: The added claim that she set the watch herself implies she knows its accuracy independently. That could be read as a reason to trust her own clock over others.

issues.quote: The low notes give the hours. Each quarter is a doubled note. The high notes give the minutes past the quarter. He worked on it for four years. He meant it to strike the first minute of the new century.
issues.fact: The sheet gives nothing about the repeater's chime mechanics, its build time, or its intended strike moment.
issues.misreading: A solver could use the invented decoding rule (hours low, quarters doubled, minutes high) to reinterpret any chime, and the four-year duration and the 'new century' target add timing hints the sheet does not support.

issues.quote: He was exact in his work and in his habits. He was not a man who would be late for anything.
issues.fact: The sheet describes the master's punctuality in no way. It mentions only his readings and that he was well when he sent her downstairs.
issues.misreading: A solver could infer that the master was reliably on time for appointments, which implies a whereabouts or timing expectation the sheet does not give.
